posts.title: Welcome to Nexatools — 30+ tools in one place
posts.excerpt: Meet Nexatools: a single, clean hub for the file, image, PDF, developer and AI tools you use every week. Here's a tour of what's inside and how we built it.
posts.content:
# Welcome to Nexatools

Every week most of us bounce between a dozen little utility sites — one for compressing an image, another for merging PDFs, a third for formatting JSON, plus whichever AI tool the group chat is talking about. **Nexatools** puts all of those in one place, behind one login, with one clean design.

## What's inside V1

- **PDF** — merge, split, compress, PDF ↔ Word, OCR, and chat with any PDF using AI.
- **Image** — resize, compress, convert to PDF, and remove backgrounds.
- **AI** — summarize, translate, rewrite, and generate speech.
- **Developer** — JSON formatter, Base64, URL encoder, JWT decoder, regex tester, hash and password generators, and more.

Every tool has its own page with a plain-English "how to use" section, an about block and an FAQ — so if you land on us from Google you get an answer, not just a form.

## Free forever for the utilities

The developer and file utilities run **entirely in your browser**. Nothing is uploaded, and there's no ads on the tool itself. You don't even need an account to use them.

The AI tools cost credits because they run on real GPUs. New accounts get 10 credits refilled daily on the Free plan; Pro ($20/month) removes the cap.

## What's next

We ship a new batch of tools every month. Next up: an image pixelator, batch renaming, a QR generator and a link shortener. If there's a tool you want, [email us](mailto:hello@nexatools.cloud) or drop a request from the dashboard.

Happy building.

posts.title: JSON formatting best practices every developer should know
posts.excerpt: Consistent JSON formatting saves debugging hours and prevents subtle bugs in APIs, configs, and logs. Here are the rules we use — and how to enforce them with the Nexatools JSON Formatter.
posts.content:
# JSON formatting best practices

JSON is deceptively simple. A single trailing comma or an unquoted key can bring down a deploy at 2 AM. Here are the seven rules we follow on every project — and how the [Nexatools JSON Formatter](/tools/json-formatter) helps you enforce them without leaving the browser.

## 1. Pick one indentation and stick with it

Two spaces is the de-facto standard for JSON in web ecosystems. Four is fine for large config files. Tabs are legal but many tools mangle them. Whatever you pick — commit it to your linter config and never mix.

## 2. Sort keys deterministically

Diffs get 10× easier to review when keys are sorted alphabetically. Most JSON linters have a `--sort-keys` flag. Do it.

## 3. No trailing commas — but comment them in your `.jsonc`

Strict JSON forbids trailing commas. VS Code style `.jsonc` allows them. Pick per file type and don't cross the streams.

## 4. Always quote keys with double quotes

Single quotes are legal JavaScript, not legal JSON. Common pitfall when pasting from a REPL.

## 5. Prefer ISO 8601 for dates

`"2026-07-19T14:32:00Z"` beats `1721399520` for readability and beats `"07/19/2026"` for portability.

## 6. Minify only at the network boundary

Store formatted JSON in your repo (diffable), minify at build time or on the wire.

## 7. Validate before you commit

A broken JSON config that reaches production is the most avoidable outage on Earth. Every JSON file should pass `JSON.parse` before it enters `main`.

## Try it now

Paste any JSON into the [Nexatools JSON Formatter](/tools/json-formatter) — it prettifies, minifies, sorts keys, and flags syntax errors with a line number. Everything runs in your browser, so it works with the most sensitive payloads too.

posts.title: 5 AI workflows that turn any PDF into a research assistant
posts.excerpt: PDFs hide most of the world's knowledge in a format designed to be printed, not read. Here are five workflows that turn any PDF into a searchable, summarizable, conversational research partner.
posts.content:
# 5 AI workflows that turn any PDF into a research assistant

Contracts. Research papers. Financial reports. Manuals. The most important documents in your life are almost always PDFs — and PDFs are almost always painful to read. Here are five workflows we use every day at Nexatools to make PDFs actually useful.

## 1. Summarize before you read

Drop the PDF into [Chat PDF](/tools/chat-pdf) and start with "Summarize this document in 5 bullet points, then list the 3 questions I should ask about it." You'll know in 30 seconds whether it's worth 30 minutes.

## 2. Extract structured data

Invoices, receipts, tables — ask "Return every line item as JSON with columns: description, quantity, unit_price, total." AI is now reliable enough to replace 90% of manual data entry.

## 3. Translate in place

Combine our [PDF-to-Word](/tools/pdf-to-word) tool with the [Translate](/tools/translate) tool to translate a document while keeping the original layout.

## 4. Compare two versions

Upload version A and version B, then ask "What are the substantive changes between these two contracts?" Faster than any diff tool and it explains the *meaning* of the change, not just the text.

## 5. Search across a folder

If you have a stack of research papers, batch-OCR the scanned ones with our [OCR tool](/tools/ocr), then feed the extracted text into Chat PDF. You now have a searchable, questionable knowledge base — no expensive vector DB required.

## The stack we recommend

1. [OCR](/tools/ocr) → make sure the PDF has real text.
2. [PDF Compressor](/tools/pdf-compressor) → keep uploads fast.
3. [Chat PDF](/tools/chat-pdf) → ask anything.
4. [Summarize](/tools/summarize) → generate briefs for teammates.
5. [Translate](/tools/translate) → cross the language gap.

All five are one click from the [Nexatools homepage](/). Free credits refill daily, no card required.
